meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The most important thing in life is to stop saying 'I wish' and start saying 'I will''?
meta.ogDescription: Not Dickens. The sentence appears in none of his books, including David Copperfield. The rival claimant is the magician who took his stage name from that novel.

answer.label: Not Charles Dickens — an unsourced modern slogan
answer.authorDates: No documented author, date or first publication
answer.sourceLine: The sentence appears nowhere in Dickens. A full-text search of 40 of his works — all fifteen novels including David Copperfield, the Christmas books, the sketches and travel writing, the collected speeches and three volumes of published letters — returns no hit for any phrase in it. Quote databases print the identical wording under David Copperfield the illusionist as readily as under Dickens, and neither camp cites a book, an interview or a date.

source.heading: The source that isn’t there

docMeta.dd: Absent from 40 Dickens titles: all 15 novels, the Christmas books, the sketches and travel writing, the speeches and the collected letters
David Copperfield, the American illusionist (b. 16 September 1956) — also uncited

source.excerpt: The most important thing in life is to stop saying ‘I wish’ and start saying ‘I will.’ Consider nothing impossible, then treat possibilities as probabilities.
trail: The only work ever named is David Copperfield, and the phrase is not in it. Checked against the Project Gutenberg text of the novel ↗, published 1849–1850, and against thirty-nine further Dickens titles: no hit for “stop saying,” “start saying,” “most important thing in life,” “consider nothing,” “nothing impossible” or “possibilities as probabilities.”

Wikiquote’s Charles Dickens page ↗ does not carry the line at all — not among the sourced quotations, and not in its Misattributed section, which lists a single entry (the “every one for himself” elephant line, credited to Charles Reade).

Where it does appear, nothing is cited. Goodreads files the full two sentences under Charles Dickens ↗ with no book named, beneath its own notice that quotes are added by the community and not verified.

The same two sentences sit on QuoteFancy under the name David Copperfield ↗, word for word and equally sourceless. That split — one text, two famous names, zero citations — is the clearest available signal of how a Victorian novelist ended up credited with a motivational slogan.
source.excerptNote: This is the full circulating form; the second sentence is usually dropped when the line is posted. It is not an extract from anything — no edition, chapter or page has ever been produced for it, by anyone, for either claimant.

source.rightsNote: No rights status can be asserted. Dickens’s own writing is long out of copyright, but that is irrelevant here because the sentence is not his: it has no identifiable author, no first publication and no date, and the competing attribution is to a performer who is still living. Treat the wording as of unknown provenance rather than as public domain.

author.name: Charles Dickens
author.heading: Charles Dickens
author.bio: Charles John Huffam Dickens (7 February 1812 – 9 June 1870) was an English writer and journalist, and the most widely read novelist of the Victorian age. He was a genuine aphorist — Micawber’s budget arithmetic and the opening of David Copperfield are his — which is exactly why unsourced uplift keeps getting hung on his name. This particular line is not among the things he wrote.

misattribution.heading: Where the credit goes, and why it’s wrong
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most-shared “Dickens” lines on the internet and one of the easiest to disprove: the only book ever named for it is David Copperfield, and the words are not in David Copperfield.

items.tag: Not in any of his works
items.why: Searched across forty Dickens titles on Project Gutenberg, including the complete text of David Copperfield ↗, with no match for any phrase in it. Wikiquote’s Dickens page ↗ does not carry it either, in any section. Goodreads prints it under his name ↗ with no book cited and a standing notice that its quotes are user-submitted and unverified.

items.scope: The title David Copperfield, read as a citation
items.why: The novel is named because the quote is filed under “David Copperfield” — not the other way round. QuoteFancy carries the identical two sentences under the bare name David Copperfield ↗ and the same text again under Charles Dickens ↗. A bare personal name that is also a book title is all it takes.

items.scope: The same two sentences, other half of the split
items.why: AZQuotes files “Stop saying ‘I wish’ and start saying ‘I will’” under a David Copperfield described as a magician born 16 September 1956 ↗, and its quote page gives no citation at all ↗. This is the likelier of the two labels, since a working motivational line fits a living performer better than a Victorian novelist — but likelier is not sourced, and it should not be reported as fact.

misattribution.truthLine: Nobody has produced a source for this sentence — not a chapter of Dickens, not an interview with the magician. Until one surfaces, the honest description is an unattributed modern slogan that acquired a Victorian author by way of a borrowed stage name ↗.

context.heading: Two famous men, one name, no page number
lead: Most fake-Dickens lines are hard to trace because the fake has no rival claimant. This one is unusually legible, because the rival claimant is right there in the filing system: the identical two sentences circulate under Charles Dickens and under David Copperfield — and David Copperfield is the title of a Dickens novel.

The living David Copperfield was born David Seth Kotkin, and Wikipedia records that he took the stage name from the Dickens novel because he liked its sound ↗. That single borrowing is enough to break a quote database. A scraper that finds “David Copperfield” with no other detail attached has two famous men to choose between, and the Victorian one carries more quotable weight. What neither attribution has ever produced is a chapter, a broadcast, or a date.
detailsBody: Sixty-eight plain-text files were pulled from Project Gutenberg, covering forty distinct Dickens titles: The Pickwick Papers, Oliver Twist, Nicholas Nickleby, The Old Curiosity Shop, Barnaby Rudge, Martin Chuzzlewit, Dombey and Son, David Copperfield, Bleak House, Hard Times, Little Dorrit, A Tale of Two Cities, Great Expectations, Our Mutual Friend and The Mystery of Edwin Drood; the five Christmas books; the sketches, Christmas stories and travel writing; Speeches: Literary and Social; and The Letters of Charles Dickens in three volumes.

Whitespace was normalised first so that a phrase broken across a line or page would still match, and each key phrase was searched case-insensitively as a regular expression rather than a literal string. Nothing matched. The novel David Copperfield uses the word “probability” freely and “probabilities” never in this construction — the search mechanism works; the phrase simply is not there.
context.pull: Dickens did write a great line about willpower in David Copperfield. It is the first sentence of the book, and it is not this one.

sourcesVerified.claim: Project Gutenberg hosts the complete text of Charles Dickens's David Copperfield, described on the page as a novel published in 1849-1850.

Wikiquote's Charles Dickens page does not contain 'The most important thing in life is to stop saying I wish and start saying I will' or 'Consider nothing impossible, then treat possibilities as probabilities' in any section; its Misattributed section lists only the 'every one for himself, and Providence for us all' line, credited to Charles Reade.

Goodreads carries the full two-sentence quote attributed to Charles Dickens with no book or source cited, alongside a notice that quotes are added by the Goodreads community and are not verified by Goodreads.
QuoteFancy carries the identical two-sentence quote under the name 'David Copperfield' with no source cited.
QuoteFancy also carries the identical two-sentence quote under the name 'Charles Dickens' with no book or source cited.
The AZQuotes author page for David Copperfield gives his occupation as magician and birth date as September 16, 1956, and includes the quote 'Stop saying I wish and start saying I will.'
AZQuotes attributes 'Stop saying I wish and start saying I will' to David Copperfield with no source, book, interview or date cited.
The illusionist was born David Seth Kotkin on September 16, 1956, and adopted the stage name David Copperfield, taken from the Charles Dickens novel, because he liked its sound.
Dickens's novel David Copperfield was serialised from May 1849 to November 1850 and published in book format in 1850.
Charles John Huffam Dickens (7 February 1812 - 9 June 1870) was an English writer and journalist, regarded as the greatest novelist of the Victorian era.

Loyola University Chicago reports doctoral research by Lydia Craig fact-checking quotes falsely attributed to Dickens, including 'What greater gift than the love of a cat!', which traces to a late-1990s self-help book rather than to Dickens, and notes that some false Dickens quotes originate in film screenplays.
